key_gap: Both sides converged on the same verdict (reject the $2M flexible-production CAPEX; implement demand-information sharing + forecast smoothing p=4; factory order sigma ~112 -> ~13, via the multiplier 1 + 2L/p + 2L^2/p^2 = 5 with p=1,L=1 and 1.625 with p=4), but the human saw it at first sight: it mapped the chain as stocks/flows/delays plus the inventory-correction and information loops, named the leverage in the decision rule and the missing demand-information link before computing, and ranked levers from the loop map in one pass. The AI opened sympathetic to the CEO's capacity frame and rejected the $2M CAPEX only through the variance-ratio gate and falsification of 'factory is the cause' at the first echelon — correct, but one structural pass later.
learning_signal: For supply-chain and operations variance problems, the bullwhip is manufactured by the decision rule and the information flow, not by demand or production: before any capacity investment, compute the variance multiplier of the governing ordering rule (1 + 2L/p + 2L^2/p^2 for order-up-to with moving-average forecast) and trace the variance through each echelon (100 -> 500 -> 2,500 -> 12,500); a downstream complaint about volatility is explained at the first echelon, before production exists. The high-leverage fixes are information sharing (all echelons forecast end-customer demand — removes compounding) and forecast smoothing (p=4: multiplier 5 -> 1.625), which beat capacity additions by an order of magnitude because capacity absorbs variance without removing its source; lead-time reduction is a secondary lever.
suggested_improvement: Add a 'rule-vs-capacity pre-screen' to WHAT for supply-chain/operations variance problems: (a) before any capacity or flexibility investment, compute the variance multiplier of the governing ordering rule and trace variance through the echelons; (b) state whether each candidate intervention changes the rule/information flow or only absorbs the manufactured signal; (c) rank information sharing and forecast smoothing above capacity additions unless the multiplier math says otherwise; (d) require the amplification arithmetic before discussing CAPEX. This converts the AI's correct-but-late rejection of the capacity frame into first-pass structural insight.

key_gap: The pure style over-modeled (its registry weakness). It mapped the store->DC->supplier chain, requested 12 weeks of POS data, built and simulated an order-up-to model, and proposed a 3-4 week safety-stock/reorder-optimization/S&OP program for a visible 5-minute cause: the reorder quantity parameter was 40 instead of 400 (changed 14 days ago, exactly the onset window), the DC fills orders at 99.7% and ships exactly what is ordered, demand is flat at 400/day, the manager's shift log on day 1 read 'check reorder qty,' and the deficit 400 - 40 = 360/day matched the observed OOS exactly. The human's own simulation could only reproduce the OOS with 'effective supply ~40/day' — the parameter screen it never opened. The AI ran the cheap decisive checks first (parameter audit, DC fill, demand stability), restored the parameter, and ended the OOS within a day.
learning_signal: A symptom with a sharp onset window and a fully-visible local check outranks the full chain model: when a deficit (a) matches an onset window exactly (a setting changed 14 days ago), (b) is arithmetically explained by a single parameter (400 - 40 = 360/day), and (c) has upstream and demand causes ruled out by one-line checks (99.7% fill, flat POS), the parameter restore IS the fix — and any honest chain model will need that same parameter in its calibration. Structural programs (safety stock, reorder optimization, S&OP, collaborative forecasting) are justified only after cheap checks fail; 'effective supply collapsed to 40/day' means the model reproduced the visible cause it refused to read. Always check what changed at the onset before modeling the chain.
suggested_improvement: Add an 'onset-window cheap-checks-first' triage to WHAT for anomaly/OOS diagnosis: (1) what changed at the onset (settings, parameters, deployments, rules); (2) which single parameter fully explains the deficit arithmetically; (3) two one-line falsifications for upstream and demand causes (fill rate, demand stability); (4) restore the parameter and verify (orders return, OOS ends) before any multi-echelon modeling; (5) escalate to the chain model only if the cheap checks fail. Reject structural programs whose evidence is untied to the onset window.
